title: Network Defense: Firewalls, Stateful Inspection & TLS 1.3
summary: Understand stateful vs stateless firewalls, VPN/Zero-Trust tunnels, and how TLS 1.3 handshake establishes verified encrypted channels.
learningObjectives: Explain TLS asymmetric key exchange switching cleanly to fast symmetric AEAD encryption
Distinguish packet filtering, stateful firewalls, WAF HTTP inspection, and IDS vs IPS

sections.heading: 1. Perimeters, Layer-7 WAF & Transport Encryption
sections.content:
Host/network firewalls filter traffic at OSI Layers 3/4 (source IP CIDR, TCP/UDP port) tracking active session state so only expected return traffic traverses cleanly. However, L3/L4 firewalls MUST permit ports 80/443 for web applications—leaving Layer-7 HTTP payloads exposed unless protected by a Web Application Firewall (WAF) and hardened backend code.

Meanwhile, TLS 1.3 protects traffic in transit against passive eavesdropping and active Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) interception: the browser validates the server's CA certificate chain and negotiates ephemeral forward-secret session keys (ECDHE) switching to hardware-accelerated AES-GCM / ChaCha20 symmetric encryption.

codeExamples.code:
Client <==1. ClientHello + Supported Ciphers==> Edge Server
       <==2. ServerHello + Cert Chain (RSA/EdDSA)==|
       (Client verifies CA Signature & Host SAN!)
       <==3. Derived Ephemeral AEAD Session Keys==> Encrypted HTTP/2 Payload
codeExamples.explanation: TLS couples certificate identity validation (asymmetric signatures) with ephemeral forward-secret symmetric transport encryption.

keyPoints: TLS encryption stops eavesdropping on Wi-Fi/ISPs; it does NOT fix authorization or SQLi vulnerabilities inside the application!
Always redirect plaintext HTTP port 80 cleanly to HTTPS 443 and send `Strict-Transport-Security` (HSTS).
commonMistakes: Disabling certificate verification (`rejectUnauthorized: false` or `curl -k`) in production scripts, opening trivial MITM compromise.

sections.heading: 2. Inspecting Certificates & Host Firewall Rules
sections.content: Engineers verify active firewall postures and certificate trust chains routinely directly from terminal diagnostics rather than guessing.

codeExamples.code:
# Verify TLS certificate chain & expiration date cleanly
openssl s_client -connect github.com:443 -servername github.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates -subject

# Restrict inbound Linux firewall strictly to HTTPS (443) and management VPN
ufw default deny incoming
ufw default allow outgoing
ufw allow 443/tcp
ufw status verbose
codeExamples.explanation: Default-deny inbound policies minimize exposed socket surfaces down strictly to intended ports.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: notBefore=... / notAfter=... and strict default-deny inbound firewall status

keyPoints: IDS alerts passively on anomalies; IPS actively drops matching malicious flows inline.
commonMistakes: Allowing database replication ports publicly instead of wrapping them over WireGuard / private VPC peering.

exercises.title: Analyze an Active Firewall & MITM Risk
exercises.objective: Fix insecure TLS flags and over-permissive firewall rules.
exercises.description: A Node microservice sets `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0` to silence a self-signed internal error, while the host opens TCP ports `0-65535` from `0.0.0.0/0`.
instructions: Explain the exact MITM attack permitted by `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0`.
Show how to resolve internal certificates safely without disabling TLS verification.
Lock down the firewall policy cleanly following default-deny inbound.
exercises.starterCode:

1. Remove NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0 -> Fix cert via: ...
2. Default-Deny Inbound Rule: ...
hints: Mount or trust the specific internal CA public root certificate rather than trusting invalid keys globally.
exercises.submissionRequirements: Complete all checklist items, test assumptions, and document verification rationale.
evaluationCriteria: Addresses the root architectural/technical challenge accurately
Follows defensive industry standards and edge-case validation
exercises.solutionExplanation: Trusting the exact internal root CA cleanly maintains verification while default-deny inbound rules eliminate stray exposed daemons.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: Why does setting `rejectUnauthorized: false` during HTTPS requests create a severe vulnerability?

options.text: It skips certificate validation so an active MITM attacker presenting any bogus certificate can intercept and modify encrypted traffic unnoticed
It prevents HTTP POST bodies from being parsed
It slows network round trips by 10x
It deletes client session cookies automatically

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Encryption without server identity verification fails to stop active MITM proxies.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: What happens under a Stateful Inspection Firewall when a client initiates an outbound HTTPS session on port 443?

options.text: The firewall logs connection state in a state table and permits established return packets back cleanly without opening port 443 inbound globally
It leaves port 443 permanently open to unsolicited internet traffic
It drops all return traffic automatically
It scans user passwords in plaintext

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Stateful firewalls track active flows and distinguish return responses from unsolicited inbound scans.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: What security benefit does HSTS (`Strict-Transport-Security`) provide?

options.text: Instructs compliant browsers never to downgrade subsequent visits to insecure plaintext HTTP

knowledgeChecks.explanation: HSTS protects users against SSL-stripping downgrade attacks.

recap: You verified TLS certificate chains, configured default-deny host firewalls, and mapped L4/L7 filtering layers.
